newsitem.title: HONG KONG: New HK bourse chief exec promises steady course.
newsitem.headline: New HK bourse chief exec promises steady course.

text.p: The next chief executive of the Stock Exchange of Hong Kong promised to steer a steady course while remaining on the alert for new challenges.
Alec Tsui, currently the exchange's deputy chief executive, said on Wednesday the bourse would definitely follow the direction laid down by outgoing chief executive Paul Chow.

"We will investigate and study in the coming few years, and the exchange will have many changes down the road," Tsui told a news conference. "We will have to face challenges and competition from...other international financial centres."
Tsui was named to a three year term effective February 1. He became deputy chief executive in January this year in charge of operation services, having joined the exchange in 1994.

Previous to that, he was a member of the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC), the industry's watchdog, for five years, rising to the level of assistant director, licensing, and general manager, human resources.

Chow, who became chief executive in 1991, presided over the introduction of share listings by mainland Chinese enterprises in Hong Kong, and made significant progress raising the transparency and disclosure levels of locally-listed companies.

Industry insiders have said his successor will have a big job further developing ties with China, a particularly sensitive task during Hong Kong's transition to Chinese-sovereignty next year. The handover takes place at midnight, June 30, 1997.
Despite the timing, exchange chairman Edgar Cheng said the 1997 issue had not been a consideration during the three-month international search for a new chief executive.

Chinese securities officials had not been consulted and would be informed of the decision on Thursday, he said. Cheng did say he had informed SFC chairman Anthony Neoh of Tsui's appointment, and that Neoh had promised to recommend necessary approval by the SFC at its meeting on Thursday.

Cheng said the exchange council had looked at 180 names provided by head hunters from inside and outside the industry and closely reviewed 50 odd candidates before asking for applications from within the bourse.
In the end, he said the council unanimously picked the deputy chief executive as the most ideal candidate.

Besides developing China ties, industry insiders have named further improving the level of transparency and disclosure and refreeing tensions between small local and large international brokerages as among the next chief executive's major tasks.
But aside from promising to follow the path laid down by Chow, Tsui himself was reluctant to reveal what his priorities were.
"I think it is premature at this point in time to say any plan or any solid action is coming down the road," he said.

Asked about concerns international investors may have about the disclosure levels of Chinese H-share companies, Tsui said such concerns would be addressed/down the road, and stressed the exchange always sought to create a level playing field.

Outgoing chief executive Paul Chow was also coy about what he planned to do after stepping down at the end of January, only saying he had not discussed a new job with anyone and planned to take leave for awhile.
